Cultures/periods Third Dynasty of Ur Production place Made in: Dilmun (historic) Excavator/field collector Excavated by: Sir Leonard Woolley (1931/32) Findspot Excavated/Findspot: Ur (historic - city) Materials steatite Technique engraved pierced Dimensions Diameter: 2.20 centimetres $Inscriptions Curator's comments Around 2100 BCE, an entrepreneurial group of merchants from the Indus Valley (possibly ‘Meluhha’ in Sumerian and Akkadian texts), settled on the island of Dilmun (modern-day Bahrain)—critically situated between their homeland and Mesopotamia. Marrying into local families and quickly acculturating to Dilmunite traditions by ca. 2050 BCE, this group of merchants came to dominate local and long-distance seafaring trade over the following centuries. From the Indus Valley these individuals brought with them important administrative technologies such as writing conventions, sealing, and the use of standard weights to Bahrain, facilitating the spread of these technologies within Dilmun culture. The wide distribution of stamp seals derived from Indus Valley types attest to the vast maritime trade network that was in operation between the late third and first half of the second millennia BCE. Changes in the seals evince the process by which Harappan and local traditions were blended together. From ca. 2600—1900 BCE, the Harappan culture of the Indus Valley utilized square stamp seals carved with an animal in profile, such as a unicorn, bull with long horns, or elephant facing right (in the impression), and below, an inscription written in Indus script (yet to be deciphered). In addition to sites such as Mohenjo-Daro, some of these seals have also been found in Mesopotamia and Oman, likely indicating the seasonal presence of Meluhhan merchants. Mesopotamian texts from this period also attest to trade relations with Dilmun, Magan (Oman), and Meluhha: rulers such as Sargon (ca. 2340-2285 BCE) and Gudea (ca. 2150-2125 BCE) boast in their inscriptions that ships from Meluhha regularly docked at Mesopotamian ports, bringing precious materials such as gemstones and wood. An Akkadian period (ca. 2340-2200 BCE) cylinder seal belonging to Shu-ilishu, ‘interpreter of the land of Meluhha’, further demonstrates the direct contact between Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley. Around 2100 BCE, circular stamp seals featuring Harappan motifs were developed by a splinter group of Meluhhan merchants who began to operate out of Bahrain. The circular shape, which is rarely found at Indus Valley sites, was likely adopted from Iran, where it was common at this time. Referred as the ‘Gulf type’, these seals remained in use until approximately 1650 BCE. They feature a semi-spherical handle that is pierced horizontally for suspension and engraved with one, two, or three parallel grooves and an image of a short-horned bull on the other side, such as the example here; they can be either inscribed or uninscribed and are predominantly made of steatite with a white glaze. Such seals are found largely in Mesopotamia and Bahrain, and more sporadically in the Indus Valley and Iran, demonstrating the presence of Dilmunite merchant communities. Variations in seal imagery, diameter, thickness, and handle height among these regions point to local production centres. The few examples of ‘Gulf type’ seals found at Indus Valley sites are indicative of Harappan interactions Mesopotamia and Bahrain. While the shape is foreign, they are otherwise quite similar to the earlier local Harappan square seals: a unicorn or a bull typically faces right (on the impression); a cult standard or a manger appears before the animal. Notably, the inscription does not follow the curve of the seal but runs straight across as it would on a square example. The inscriptions on ‘Gulf type’ seals from Iran and the Indus Valley find parallels with other Harrapan inscriptions, although they cannot be translated. ‘Gulf type’ seals found in Mesopotamia—such as this seal from Ur—and Bahrain became increasingly removed from Indus traditions. In earlier examples, such as the one illustrated here, the bull, now short-horned still faces right (in the impression), but with time, this convention is abandoned; in the same manner, the manger becomes replaced with a bale of fodder and eventually disappears altogether (as seen here), along with the standard; other animals such as caprids and scorpions are introduced.Based on the findspots of these seals it is possible to postulate that inscribed seals were used by merchants involved in long-distance trade – as they are found in Mesopotamia, Bahrain, and the Indus Valley – while uninscribed examples were used by those operating more locally on Bahrain. This seal was found in PG 1847—one of a row of shaft-graves discovered next to the mausolea of Third Dynasty of Ur (2112-2004 BCE) kings in the cemetery area of the city in southern Iraq. This shaft contained nineteen burials. Because the seal was excavated from the fill of the shaft, it is unclear whether it was a funerary deposit that belonged to one of the burials. The excavator, Sir Leonard Woolley, hypothesized, however, that it may have been placed in the fill as an offering when the grave was closed up—thus, associated with the burial(s). In any case, the fill and the burials can be dated to the same time period. Three wooden coffins with pitched-roof lids were found at the bottom of the shaft-grave. The individuals in these coffins wore gold fillets, hair ribbons, hair-rings, and earrings; strings of beads of semi-precious stones; and gold, silver, and copper bracelets. The grave goods accompanying them included copper weapons and vessels in addition to pottery. Higher up in the shaft were sixteen simpler burials—featuring either smaller quantities of similar goods or none at all.Bibliographic references Gadd 1932a / Seals of ancient Indian style found at Ur (pp.13-14, pl.III: 16 and pp.201-202) Gadd 1933a / Antiquities from Ur: temporary exhibition (p.43) Woolley et al 1934a / The Royal Cemetery (p.593, pl.211) Mitchell T C 1986a / Indus and Gulf type seals from Ur (no.2, p.279, fig. 107) Location Not on display Exhibition history 2025-2028 13 Dec-30 Nov, Mumbai, CSMVS, Networks of the Past: A Study Gallery of India and the Ancient World 2019 15 May-9 Sep, Hong Kong Heritage Museum, 'A History of the World in 100 Objects' 2018 19 Apr-22 Jul, Musée des Beaux-Arts, Valenciennes, 'A History of the World in 100 Objects' 2017 28 Jun-08 Oct, Shanghai Museum, Shanghai, 'A History of the World in 100 Objects' 2017 1 Mar-31 May, National Museum of China, Beijing, 'A History of the World in 100 Objects' 2016-2017 08 Sep-29 Jan, National Museum of Australia, Canberra, 'A History of the World in 100 Objects' 2016 13 Feb-18 Jun, National Museum of Western Australia, Perth, 'A History of the World in 100 Objects' 2015-2016 20 Sep-11 Jan, Kobe City Museum, Kobe, 'A History of the World in 100 Objects' 2015 14 Jul–6 Sep, Kyushu National Museum, Dazaifu, 'A History of the World in 100 Objects' 2015 18 Apr–28 Jun, Tokyo Metropolitan Art Museum, Tokyo, 'A History of the World in 100 Objects' 2014-2015 13 Dec-15 Mar, National Palace Museum, Taipei, 'A History of the World in 100 Objects' 2014 23 Apr-01 Aug, Manarat Al Saadiyat, Abu Dhabi, 'A History of the World in 100 Objects’ 2000, Tokyo, 'Indus Valley' 1996 17 Jan-31 Dec, Israel, Jerusalem, Bible Lands Museum, Jerusalem : A Capital for all Times. Imported Indus artefacts, such as carnelian beads or ivory artefacts attest to exchanges between Mesopotamia and its distant neighbour, however the presence of rectangular Indus seals at Mesopotamian sites hints at a more invasive mercantile presence. L1680@P26: seals that were recovered all came from Site Levels II
L1681@P26: and III, which roughly correspond to Qala’at
L1682@P26: al-Bahrain periods IIb and IIc, respectively. The
L1683@P26: excavators are confident that these Gulf Type seals
L1684@P26: are either intrusive from the late third-millennium
L1685@P26: deposits or, as suggested by Crawford, that ‘their
L1686@P26: presence could be explained as that of survivals or
L1687@P26: heirlooms’ (2001: 39).
L1688@P26: The substantial negative evidence for Gulf Type
L1689@P26: seals from the Saar settlement thus confirms the
L1690@P26: observations from Qala’at al-Bahrain, and the conclusion is that the utilisation of Gulf Type seals in
L1691@P26: settlements on Bahrain Island was generally confined to Qala’at al-Bahrain period IIa (2050–2000 BC)
L1692@P26: after which they were more or less abruptly replaced
L1693@P26: by seals of the Dilmun Type in Qala’at al-Bahrain
L1694@P26: period IIb. Furthermore, since the Dilmun Type is
L1695@P26: securely linked to the historical sequence of Mesopotamia by the famous impression of a style I seal on
L1696@P26: a tablet dated to the tenth year in the reign of king
L1697@P26: Gungunum of Larsa (1923 BC) (Hallo & Buchanan
L1698@P26: 1965; Kjærum 1980), a launch date of the Dilmun
L1699@P26: Type around 2000 BC appears solidly founded.
L1700@P26: Given the combined evidence it would thus seem
L1701@P26: that one should consider the length of any transitory
L1702@P26: period where the Gulf and Dilmun Type seals
L1703@P26: coexisted to have been fairly brief.
L1704@P26: The observations from the Early Dilmun settlements in Bahrain are complemented by evidence
L1705@P26: from the Early Dilmun burial mounds from where
L1706@P26: new evidence has recently been presented (Laursen,
L1707@P26: in press). This demonstrates that in Bahrain the Gulf
L1708@P26: Type seals appeared in the tombs exactly at the time
L1709@P26: when the burial praxis changed from scattered
L1710@P26: cairn-like mounds of Early Type to Late Type
L1711@P26: conical mounds concentrated in vast mound cemeteries (see Lowe 1986 for similar conclusions).
L1712@P26: Through an analysis of the ‘horizontal’ stratigraphy
L1713@P26: of the Karzakkan Cemetery based on changing
L1714@P26: patterns in burial mound architecture and pottery
L1715@P26: and seal distributions, it was additionally demonstrated that Gulf Type seals clustered in the largest
L1716@P26: of presumably numerous ‘proto-cemeteries’. After
L1717@P26: the burial mounds had accumulated in this ‘protocemetery’ they became surrounded by later burials,
L1718@P26: many of which now featured seals of Dilmun Type.
L1719@P26: Two of the seals with Indus text (Fig. 9 ⁄ 8, 56) were
L1720@P26: found in the cluster of Gulf Type seals in this ‘protocemetery’. The combination of inscribed and uninscribed Gulf Type seals observed in the Karzakkan
L1721@P26: Cemetery is analogous to that which could be
L1722@P26: observed in the period IIa deposits at Qala’at alBahrain, but unfortunately the data from the Karzakkan cemetery is not sufficient to elucidate further
L1723@P26: on the chronological relationship between these two
L1724@P26: Gulf Type variants.
L1725@P26: From Failaka Island on the north-western fringe of
L1726@P26: the Dilmun sphere, the chronological evidence on the
L1727@P26: Gulf Type is chiefly negative. Here only two examples (exclusive of the Dilmun Type seal with pseudoIndus script [Fig. 9 ⁄ 13]) have been reported — a
L1728@P26: number that is in striking contrast to the approximately 500 seals of Dilmun Type that have so far been
L1729@P26: unearthed from this small island. The Failaka evidence clearly strengthens the general assumption
L1730@P26: that the two seal types were chronologically separated. This is underscored by the unique Dilmun seal
L1731@P26: with unparalleled ‘Indus’ script (Fig. 9 ⁄ 13), which,
L1732@P26: with its bull’s head⁄ eye carved in the classic compass
L1733@P26: STEFFEN TERP LAURSEN
L1734@P26-27: 122drill technique, moreover conforms to Kjærum’s later
L1735@P27: Dilmun glyptic style I (1994). On the whole this seal
L1736@P27: definitely stands out as later than the Gulf Type seals
L1737@P27: but remains somewhat enigmatic both because of the
L1738@P27: alien⁄unparalleled signs in the inscription and the
L1739@P27: abnormally large diameter. This seal and, for that
L1740@P27: matter, also seal no. 12 from Failaka, may very well
L1741@P27: represent ‘replicas’ made from the models of heavily
L1742@P27: curated⁄heirloom seals with Indus inscription.
L1743@P27: The Gulf Type-related seal from Tepe Yahya
L1744@P27: (Table 1, no. 119) was found in the ‘Persian Gulf
L1745@P27: room’ that is ascribed to phase IVB5 by Potts, who
L1746@P27: dates this phase to the last centuries of the third
L1747@P27: millennium BC (Potts 2001: 105). This position is,
L1748@P27: however, challenged by Lamberg-Karlovsky who
L1749@P27: argues for a date from 2400 to 2100 BC of phase IVB
L1750@P27: (Lamberg-Karlovsky 2001: 276). In respect of Lamberg-Karlovsky’s objection to Potts’s dating of phase
L1751@P27: IVB5, he proffers the ‘Persian Gulf’ seal as an
L1752@P27: argument of his higher chronology rather than the
L1753@P27: lower chronology suggested by Potts. In LambergKarlovsky’s argumentation it appears that he has
L1754@P27: misread the conclusions of Mitchell (1986) because
L1755@P27: he advances Mitchell’s 1986 paper in a claim that the
L1756@P27: ‘Persian Gulf’ type is of pre-Akkadian date (Lamberg-Karlovsky 2001: 274), for which the evidence
L1757@P27: certainly does not provide any reasonable support.
L1758@P27: Potts has subsequently presented more evidence for
L1759@P27: lowering the regional Kerman chronology including
L1760@P27: that of the Bampur sequence, based among others,
L1761@P27: on the black-on-grey canisters found in the welldated tomb at Tell Abraq (Potts 2003).
L1762@P27: At any rate, if one accepts that the ‘Persian Gulf
L1763@P27: room’ seal is a creation of the ‘Gulf tradition’, which
L1764@P27: I am inclined to do, its presence would certainly
L1765@P27: lower the date of Tepe Yahya phase IVB5 rather than
L1766@P27: raise it. The conclusion must be that until the local
L1767@P27: Kerman chronology is improved, limited faith can
L1768@P27: be vested in the prospect of the Tepe Yahya seal
L1769@P27: clarifying the chronology of the Gulf Type. However, with considerable reservation a date of the seal
L1770@P27: to c.2150–2050 BC is proposed here.
L1771@P27: The fact that the seals of Group 4 are the ones
L1772@P27: which bear the closest morphological resemblance to
L1773@P27: Dilmun Type seals implies that they generally date
L1774@P27: in the later part of the Gulf Type sequence. This
L1775@P27: finds additional support in the high frequency in
L1776@P27: Group 4 of the seals with bull in profile without
L1777@P27: inscription as well as seals carved in the ‘local’ style.

L1784@P27: THE WESTWARD TRANSMISSION OF INDUS VALLEY SEALING TECHNOLOGY
L1785@P27-28: 123Geographical distribution and discussion
L1786@P28: Observing the accumulated distribution of all currently known circular seals of Gulf and Dilmun type
L1787@P28: one is struck by the vastness of its geographic range
L1788@P28: (Fig. 13). While some seals possibly travelled beyond the borders of the network of the Gulf trade in
L1789@P28: the hands of non-Dilmun agents, most seals probably testify to the actual degree of integration of
L1790@P28: Dilmun into an immense network of long-distance
L1791@P28: exchange. However, during the almost 500 years
L1792@P28: (c.2100–1650 BC) in which the circular stamp seals
L1793@P28: were in use, this dynamic network underwent a
L1794@P28: number of substantial changes.
L1795@P28: In this study the focus has been on the emergence
L1796@P28: of sealing technology in Arabia and as will be
L1797@P28: evident, the geographical distributions of the major
L1798@P28: Gulf Type variants prove particularly instructive on
L1799@P28: this development.
L1800@P28: At this point it can hardly be disputed that
L1801@P28: stamp-seal technology, either directly or indirectly,
L1802@P28: was transmitted from the Indus Valley, and it is
L1803@P28: consequently necessary first to consult the distribution of classic square Harappan seals in the
L1804@P28: ‘west’. The number of actual Harappan sealing
L1805@P28: implements in the Near East and Arabia is limited,
L1806@P28: but importantly concentrated in Mesopotamia.
L1807@P28: Discounting the western periphery of the Harappan
L1808@P28: sphere, a mere seven classic square seals have been
L1809@P28: found which correspond to those of the Indus
L1810@P28: Valley and of these, six come from Mesopotamia
L1811@P28: while one slightly atypical specimen of copper has
L1812@P28: been recovered in eastern Oman14 (Fig. 14 with
L1813@P28: references). Considering the amount of fieldwork
L1814@P28: carried out over the last fifty years on the Oman
L1815@P28: peninsula and on Bahrain, one should not expect
L1816@P28: this picture to change considerably. The occurrence
L1817@P28: of these seals in Mesopotamia has repeatedly been
L1818@P28: seen in connection with the presence of Meluhhan
L1819@P28: Fig. 13.
L1820@P28: The distribution of Gulf and Dilmun Type seals demonstrates the geographical vastness of the underlying networks of exchanges.
L1821@P28: 14 As noted by A. Parpola (1994a: 315) the copper square
L1822@P28: seals from Ra’s al-Hadd and Ur differ in material from
L1823@P28: the steatite conventionally used for seals in the Indus
L1824@P28: Valley, a fact which could also suggest that these particular seals were manufactured in some as yet unidentified
L1825@P28: production centre located between the two regions. A.
L1826@P28: Parpola suggests Oman as the origin on account of the
L1827@P28: material being copper. However, since steatite is also
L1828@P28: plentifully available here and because this part of Arabia
L1829@P28: did not develop a significant independent sealing technology, the exact origin of the rarer square seals of copper
L1830@P28: appears unresolved.
